children: The following are expectations for the resumption of grain and soy complex trading at the Chicago Board of Trade at 8:30 a.m. CDT (1330 GMT) on Thursday.
WHEAT - Down 18 to 32 cents per bushel
CBOT wheat
sharply lower in a profit-taking retreat from multi-year highs after Russian President
said there was a chance of a peace agreement to end the
A steep drop in Black Sea grain exports and weather concerns about European crops had lifted benchmark wheat futures
to the highest since February 2023 earlier this week.

Asian wheat importers have bought at least half a million metric tons of Australian and Argentine wheat in recent deals, three trade sources said, as buyers scramble to replace Black Sea cargoes delayed by attacks on vessels and grain export infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia issued a tender to buy 535,000 metric tons of wheat for delivery from November through December, the country's General Food Security Authority said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported U.S. wheat export sales in the week ended August 27 at 313,500 metric tons, in line with trade estimates for 350,000 to 650,000 tons.
CBOT December soft red winter wheat (WZ26) was last down 31-1/4 cents at $7.42-3/4 per bushel.
K.C. December hard red winter wheat (KWZ26) was last down 29 cents at $8.05-1/4 a bushel. Minneapolis December spring wheat (MWEZ26) was last 23-3/4 cents lower at $7.58-1/4 a bushel.
CORN - Down 7 to 13 cents
CBOT corn

lower on spillover pressure from lower wheat and profit taking after reaching a three-year high earlier this week. Strong export demand and concerns about lower U.S. corn yields are limiting declines.

The USDA said new-crop U.S. corn export sales in the week ended August 27 are at 1,986,400 metric tons, above trade estimates for 500,000 to 1,600,000 tons. The agency also reported net cancellations of 829,600 tons of old-crop sales.
CBOT December corn (CZ26) was last down 12-1/2 cents at $5.31 per bushel.
SOYBEANS - Down 10 to 15 cents
CBOT soybeans

lower for a second straight session on spillover pressure from lower wheat and profit taking after hitting the highest point since December 2023 earlier this week. Strong export demand from China is limiting declines.

The USDA said new-crop U.S. soybean export sales in the week ended August 27 are at 1,948,400 metric tons, in line with trade estimates for 1,400,000 to 2,500,000 tons. The agency also reported net cancellations of 94,200 tons of old-crop sales.

CBOT November soybeans (SX26) were last down 12 cents at $12.98-1/4 per bushel.
